summary: Describes 6a44, an experimental way to give native IPv6 connectivity to sites behind IPv4-only customer equipment that does a NAT. It is meant to address limitations of Teredo, which works without an ISP's involvement but has limits in connectivity with native IPv6 addresses.

eli5.summary: If your house only has an old road, you can still get to the new highway through a special tunnel. 6a44 builds that tunnel with help from the internet company.

questions: how to get ipv6 behind an ipv4 nat
how to get ipv6 behind ipv4 nat
subtitle: A way to provide native IPv6 through an ISP tunnel when behind an IPv4-only router.

tldr.problem: Sites with IPv4-only CPE (customer equipment) have limited IPv6 options. Teredo provides some access but relies on third-party servers and cannot guarantee connectivity between Teredo and native IPv6 addresses. Solutions that require manual configuration are not practical for deployment at scale.
tldr.mechanism: 6a44 creates native IPv6 addresses by encoding the client's external IPv4 address and port in an IPv6 prefix assigned by the ISP. Clients tunnel IPv6 packets through UDP/IPv4 to 6a44 relays, which forward to the native IPv6 network. No third-party servers needed; the ISP manages the infrastructure.
tldr.outcome: The specification is experimental; its status depends on whether major ISPs choose to support it. It is positioned as a complementary solution to Teredo, not a replacement.

today: RFC 6751 remains experimental. Deployment depends on ISP support, which has been limited. It serves as a technical specification for sites seeking an alternative to Teredo where ISP cooperation is available.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Many customer sites still have IPv4-only CPE (routers) due to the large installed base of older equipment. Without IPv6, these hosts cannot reach the modern internet fully. Configured tunnels like 6to4 require manual registration and create inefficient paths where local traffic must traverse distant servers. Teredo works without ISP involvement but has limitations: connectivity with native IPv6 is uncertain, some NAT types break Teredo-to-Teredo communication, and it requires well-known Teredo servers.

6a44 takes the approach that proved successful for 6rd: involve the ISP. The ISP assigns a /48 IPv6 prefix to its 6a44 network and operates 6a44 relays on its own network. This enables direct connectivity to the native IPv6 internet and local, efficient paths between 6a44 clients in the same site.
sections.eli5: 6a44 is like a special program where your internet company helps you. Instead of going through strangers' servers, you go through your company's tunnel, and everything is faster and more reliable.

sections.title: How 6a44 Addresses Work
sections.content:
A 6a44 IPv6 address encodes four pieces of information that together identify the client and allow packets to reach it:

1. ISP prefix (48 bits): The /48 IPv6 prefix assigned by the ISP to its 6a44 network.

2. Client's external IPv4 address (32 bits): The IPv4 address (global or private) assigned to the customer site by the ISP or carrier, after passing through any NAT boxes.

3. Tunnel mapped port (16 bits): The external UDP port assigned by the NAT when the client opens its tunnel, allowing replies to return to the right place.

4. Client's local IPv4 address (32 bits): The private IPv4 address assigned to the client within the site, enabling communication with other 6a44 clients that share the same external address.

This design allows an IPv6 address to be computed by the client and confirmed by the relay, with no prior registration.
sections.eli5: Your 6a44 address is made from three parts: the tunnel company's prefix, your current location (address and port), and your home address inside your network. That's all the relay needs to find you.

sections.title: Client and Relay Operation
sections.content:
A 6a44 client starts by sending a bubble (a special UDP/IPv4 packet with the client's computed IPv6 prefix) to the 6a44 relay address (an anycast IPv4 address and port reserved by IANA). The relay responds with a bubble containing the client's assigned IPv6 prefix, confirming the mapping. The client periodically sends bubbles to maintain the NAT mapping and detect when it changes (due to NAT reset or CPE reboot).

For IPv6 packets to other 6a44 clients in the same site, the client encapsulates them directly in IPv4 (not through the relay). For packets to destinations outside the site, the client encapsulates them in UDP/IPv4 and sends them to the relay. The relay either forwards to another 6a44 client (if the destination is encoded in the packet) or decapsulates and sends via native IPv6 to the global internet.
sections.eli5: Your computer sends a knock on the relay's door with your address code. The relay confirms it, and then you can send messages locally within your site or through the relay to the rest of the world.

sections.title: Deployment Models and Scalability
sections.content:
6a44 works in two ISP network models: global IPv4, where each customer site gets a public IPv4 address, and private IPv4 (NAT444), where the ISP itself runs NAT boxes and assigns private addresses. In both cases, the client's 6a44 address encodes the IPv4 it sees after the CPE NAT, and the ISP's relays are reachable at the well-known anycast address 192.88.99.2 on port 1027.

The ISP relays are completely stateless: they compute locator mappings on demand from the IPv6 address, require no persistent per-client database, and scale independently of client count. Clients are also stateless from an infrastructure perspective; they need only know the anycast relay address, not specific server identities.
sections.eli5: Whether your company is simple or has multiple NAT layers, 6a44 still works. The relay doesn't need to remember anything about you; it just looks at your address and knows what to do.

sections.title: Comparison with Teredo and Alternatives
sections.content:
6a44 shares Teredo's goal of providing IPv6 without CPE upgrades, but differs in key ways. Teredo uses a well-known prefix (2001:0::/32) and requires coordination with Teredo servers that are often far away, resulting in inefficient paths and uncertain connectivity to native IPv6 networks. 6a44 uses ISP-assigned prefixes and relays on the ISP's own network, providing direct, efficient paths.

Like 6rd (the improvement over 6to4), 6a44 sacrifices independence—it requires ISP cooperation—in exchange for reliability, efficiency, and clear operational boundaries. It coexists with other solutions: sites may deploy 6a44 alongside Teredo or configured tunnels, with clients choosing the mechanism that works best for each destination.
sections.eli5: Teredo is like a backup system run by volunteers. 6a44 is like your own internet company building the tunnel for you. Better for real use, but only if your company agrees to help.
